s: The apostles greet the Church in the name of the Trinity and set out to give the rules Christ commanded them, each apostle speaking in turn.
John: we will answer for what was given to us, so show no favouritism. Love God, and love your neighbour as yourself.
Matthew: do not do to your neighbour what you would not want done to you.
Do not steal, practise magic or astrology, kill a child before or after birth, covet or hate. Love others more than yourself.
Andrew: flee evil and do not be angry, for anger leads to murder.
Philip: do not be lustful, for lust leads to adultery. The demons of anger and lust ruin the soul.
Simon: do not speak evil or look proudly.
James: do not practise divination, charms or the reading of omens, for all this leads to idolatry.
Nathanael: do not lie or love money and vainglory, for these lead to theft.
Judas: do not grumble or be harsh. Be gentle and accept everything that happens as from God.
Thomas: honour the one who taught you the word of God, and support him, for the worker deserves his wage.
Cephas: do not cause division but make peace. Judge fairly, without favouring the rich, and share with the needy.
Bartholomew: do good while there is time, for the day of God is near. The apostles ask Peter to speak.
How to choose a bishop where there are few believers, with the help of neighbouring churches, and how the people should obey him.
A reader is ordained after testing. He must be sober, quiet, of good character and must practise what he reads.
Deacons are ordained on the witness of the people. They must have one wife and have raised their children well.
Three widows are ordained: two to pray for the afflicted and one to care for sick women.
Deacons should do good works day and night, care for the poor and not favour the rich.
The lay people should obey their clergy gladly, keep their own place and live in peace with one another.
The apostles declare that the Oblation is truly the Body and Blood of Christ, as the Lord said at the Last Supper.
Whether women may serve at the altar: the apostles answer that they should pray and help the needy. The end of the first collection.
The ordination of a bishop, chosen by all the people, with the prayer of ordination and the full prayer of the Oblation, the Eucharist.
The ordination of a presbyter, with the bishop's prayer over him.
The ordination of a deacon by the bishop alone, since he is ordained to serve and not for the priesthood.
A confessor who suffered chains for Christ already has the honour of the presbyterate. Prayer may be offered freely by those of right faith.
Widows are appointed by being named, not by laying on of hands, and only after long testing. Their office is prayer.
A reader receives the book, and virgins and subdeacons are not ordained by laying on of hands. A gift of healing must first be proven.
Newcomers who want baptism are questioned about their life and work. Some occupations must be given up, such as idol-making and the theatre.
Soldiers, magistrates, magicians and others: what they must give up to be received.
Rules for those who live with a concubine: a faithful concubine may be received, but a man must marry or give her up.
Catechumens hear instruction for three years, though good conduct may shorten the time.
Catechumens pray apart from the faithful and do not give the kiss of peace. Women stand apart and veil their heads.
The teacher lays hands on the catechumens and dismisses them. A catechumen killed for Christ is baptized in his own blood.
Those ready for baptism are examined on their life, exorcised and prepared by fasting and a night vigil.
The order of baptism at cock-crow: renouncing Satan, anointing, the threefold profession of faith, and the first Eucharist with milk and honey.
Widows and virgins fast and pray. The blessed bread shared at meals is not the Eucharist.
Thanks is given over the cup before meals. Catechumens may receive blessed bread but not the Eucharist.
When the bishop speaks at the common meal all are silent. Laymen may not bless the bread.
Those who invite widows to a meal should send them home before evening.
On the gifts God gives the Church, and a second full order of baptism, with its prayers over the water, the oil and the newly baptized.
The blessing of first fruits offered in church, and which fruits may be blessed.
During the Paschal fast none may eat before the proper time. Exceptions for the sick, the pregnant and travellers.
Deacons tell the bishop who is sick, so that he may visit them.
On rising, the faithful wash their hands and pray, and go to hear instruction in the church when it is given.
The faithful receive the Eucharist before tasting any food.
The Eucharist must be guarded with care so that none of it falls or is lost, for it is the Body of Christ.
Deacons and presbyters gather each day with the bishop to pray and receive his instructions.
No one should be charged for burial in the common grave of the poor. The bishop pays those who keep it.
The hours of prayer through the day and night and what each recalls of Christ's Passion. Sealing the forehead with the sign of the cross.
No one should boast of a gift or office. Christ gave the Church its gifts for the salvation of Jews and Gentiles.
Those in authority should not despise those under them, and bishops should not exalt themselves over their people.
Not all who prophesy or cast out demons are holy. Even Balaam and Caiaphas prophesied.
A false bishop is no bishop. Prophets are to be tested. How the faithful are seated in church and how visitors are received.
The ordination of a bishop chosen from the people, and the order of the holy Oblation.
The ordination of presbyters and deacons by the bishop.
A confessor is not ordained for having confessed, though he deserves great honour. One who denies Christ is deposed.
Virgins and widows are not ordained by laying on of hands.
A bishop must be ordained by two or three bishops, not by one.
What belongs to the bishop: to bless, to ordain and to offer the Oblation. What presbyters and deacons may do.
Deaconesses keep the doors of the church and help at the baptism of women, but do not bless.
First fruits go to the clergy, and tithes to the other ministers, virgins, widows and the poor.
How the blessed bread left over is shared among the bishop, presbyters, deacons and others.
Those who wish to receive the holy mysteries are brought to the bishop and examined on their life.
Converts are examined about their work and the testimony of their masters. Forbidden trades must be given up.
Rules on concubines for new converts. A layman who teaches well may teach.
On rising, the faithful wash their hands and pray. Masters must treat their servants fairly.
The faithful and their servants rest on the Sabbath and on the Lord's Day, to go to church and hear the Scriptures.
No work in Holy Week and Easter week, nor on the Ascension, Pentecost and the feasts of the Lord and the apostles. Honour the martyrs.
Pray at dawn, at the third, sixth and ninth hours, in the evening, at bedtime, at midnight and at cock-crow.
When unbelievers prevent you from going to church, pray at home. Flee from the assemblies of the impious.
The dead are remembered with psalms and prayers on the third, seventh and thirtieth days and on the anniversary.
Those who flee persecution for the faith are to be received with honour. Against those who seek ordination for gain.
The order of the priesthood and the prayers of the Church: for the sick, travellers, the poor, the rains and rivers, the catechumens and the dead.

i: The Sinodos is a collection of church rules, called canons, which the Ethiopian Church counts in its broader New Testament. It has four parts. This is the second and best known, the Te’ezaz or Statutes, which presents itself as the teaching of the twelve apostles, each speaking in turn.

Most of it comes from ancient church orders written in Greek in the second to fourth centuries, above all the Apostolic Tradition, a guide to church life linked to Saint Hippolytus of Rome (around AD 215). So it gives a rare look at how the early Church worked: how bishops, priests and deacons were ordained, how converts were taught for three years before baptism, which jobs they had to give up, how baptism and the first Eucharist were celebrated (with milk and honey for the newly baptized), and when to fast and pray.

What to expect: 72 numbered statutes, some a single sentence, some long prayers. The Catholic Church does not count it among the books of the Bible, though its sources are treasured witnesses to early Christian worship.
